Sierpinski Gasket via Chaos Game

ProbabilitySequences
Game: A dot hops halfway towards a corner picked at random, again and again. Watch what picture the dots make.
How to play: Press Start, and lower the Delay to go faster. Drag a corner to change the triangle.

Move with arrow keys:
Look for the math

The chaos game draws a perfectly regular picture, the Sierpinski gasket, by random means.

Three maps

For a point x let FA(x) = (x + A)/2, the point halfway from x to A, and likewise FB and FC. Each shrinks the whole triangle to half its size in one corner. The three half-size copies cover the triangle except for a hole in the middle; doing it again leaves nine copies and four holes, and so on for ever. What survives is the gasket: the one shape made of three half-size copies of itself.

Why the dots avoid the holes

The game starts at a corner, which is in the gasket, and each map sends the gasket into itself, so every later dot is in the gasket too. The logic test tried all 59,049 runs of ten random choices: every dot passed the test of belonging to the gasket twelve levels deep, and the middle hole was never touched.

Why the dots fill it

The last k choices decide which of the 3k small copies the dot is in: the last corner picked is the big copy, the one before it the copy inside that, and so on. Since every string of choices turns up sooner or later, every small copy gets dots. This is Elton's ergodic theorem for iterated function systems in miniature; the test found 40,000 dots enough to visit all 729 copies of size 1/64.

Turn on Show iterations with a long delay to follow single moves, then set the delay to 0 and squash the triangle flat.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
